---
title: Transpiration and water in plants
lang: en
free: true
---
Transpiration is the continuous loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, primarily through microscopic pores called stomata on the undersides of leaves. Far from being mere water waste, transpiration is the engine that pulls water and dissolved minerals from the soil up through the entire plant body. On a warm day a single large tree can transpire hundreds of litres of water.

## Water uptake and the xylem pathway
Water enters a plant through root hair cells by osmosis, moving from regions of higher water potential in moist soil into root cells. From there it travels across the root cortex and into the xylem — a network of hollow, lignified tubes that extend from root tips to the highest leaves. The xylem conducts water as a continuous column under tension. Because water molecules are strongly cohesive, the evaporation of water at the leaf surface pulls the entire column upward, a mechanism known as the cohesion-tension theory.

## Stomata and environmental control
Stomata are flanked by pairs of guard cells that regulate pore opening. When water is plentiful and light is available, guard cells inflate with water, bowing outward and widening the pore; carbon dioxide can then diffuse in for use in the leaf while water vapour escapes. In drought conditions the hormone abscisic acid signals guard cells to deflate, closing stomata and drastically reducing transpiration to conserve water.
